title: Pride of birth
hook: a proud young brahmin insults the Sakyans, and his own ancestry comes out
carry: no talk of birth at the summit

segments.voice: Yesterday: accaya, a wrong seen as wrong, and your line, regret, confessed. Today ends a week, with a young man very proud of his family.

A famous brahmin teacher named Pokkharasati wants to know if the Buddha is really who people say. So he sends his student, Ambattha, a young man who has mastered the Vedas. Ambattha arrives and doesn't sit down. He walks around while the Buddha sits, talking at him. And when the Buddha asks if that's how he speaks to elders, Ambattha starts on the Sakyans, the Buddha's own clan. Once, he says, I went to their assembly hall in Kapilavatthu, and they laughed, and nobody offered me a seat. They're menials.
screen: `POKKHARASATI SENDS HIS STUDENT.` → `AMBATTHA WON'T SIT DOWN.` → `THE SAKYANS LAUGHED AT ME.`

segments.voice: The Buddha's first reply is gentle. Even a little quail can chirp as it likes in its own nest; Kapilavatthu is the Sakyans' home. But Ambattha insults them again, and again. So the Buddha asks a simple question: what's your clan? Kanhayana, says Ambattha. And the Buddha tells the old story. The Sakyans trace their line to an ancient king, Okkaka. That king had a slave woman, and she had a son named Kanha. Ambattha's clan descends from him. By the standards Ambattha himself has been using, his own ancestor was the son of a slave in the Sakyans' royal house. Ambattha won't answer at first. The text says a spirit holding a thunderbolt appeared above him, and he finally admits: yes, that's what my teachers say. His fellow students start jeering. And here's the turn. The Buddha stops them. Don't look down on Ambattha, he says. That Kanha became a great sage, and a king gave him his own daughter in marriage. So the story doesn't end as a humiliation. Read this way, it shows that pride of birth falls apart when you look closely. The Pali word is jati: birth. Then the teaching. In the highest knowledge and conduct, there's no talk of birth, no talk of clan, no talk of who is worthy of whom. That talk belongs to marriages and family arrangements. Look back at the week: the moonlit ride, the dodging answers, honored, wings, the gem and thread, regret confessed. And now a family tree, shaken.
screen: `A QUAIL CHIRPS IN ITS OWN NEST` · `WHAT'S YOUR CLAN?` · `DON'T LOOK DOWN ON HIM` · `NO TALK OF BIRTH AT THE SUMMIT` · then, large: `PRIDE OF BIRTH.`

segments.voice: If a pride of family comes to mind, our people, our name, our side of town, our school, hold it gently and notice any small lift it gives. Then picture the family tree going back past anyone you know, to people of every kind, and let the lift soften; you can keep loving your family and just set down the ranking.
Jati. Birth, also the group one is born into: it matters to marriages and family trees, and not at all to knowledge and good conduct.
Your line: no talk of birth at the summit. What counts there is knowledge and conduct. Day five hundred thirty-two, done.

howItsDone: In Buddhist monastic communities, people from every background ordain together, and order is counted from ordination, not birth; the teaching that conduct, not lineage, makes a person noble is repeated across the discourses.

fork.setup: Ambattha has finally admitted his clan's ancestry, and his fellow students are jeering at him. you're the Buddha. what do you do?
options: tell them not to look down on him, and praise his ancestor.
join in to drive the lesson home.
fork.reveal: the Buddha defends him: Kanha became a great sage, and a king gave him his daughter. the point was the emptiness of pride, not Ambattha's shame.

original.note: Pali and Sanskrit jati: birth, also the group one is born into. the ground of Ambattha's pride.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Buddha simply out-argued a rude young man.
what it means: he showed that pride of birth falls apart when traced back, and then defended the young man from mockery.

what a scholar hears: the Ambattha Sutta preserves an origin story of the Sakyans from King Okkaka (Ikshvaku), and its closing verse ranks knowledge and conduct above all lineage among gods and humans.

chat.says: Didn't the Buddha care at all about which family you come from?
options: Birth matters for marriages, he said, not in the highest knowledge and conduct.
He said only the Sakyans, his own clan, could ever reach the summit.
He said a slave's descendants could never grow into great sages.
chat.meaning: Ambattha's pride falls apart when the old story is told. In the highest knowledge and conduct, the Buddha says, there's no talk of birth or clan.

Ambattha.meaning: a proud young brahmin student sent to test the Buddha

Vedas.meaning: the ancient sacred verses the brahmins mastered

jati.meaning: birth, and the group one is born into

notes: DN 3 paraphrased. Confirm: Ambattha walking while the Buddha sits; the Kapilavatthu assembly-hall complaint; the quail simile; the clan name Kanhayana; Okkaka's slave woman (Disa) and her son Kanha; the yakkha Vajirapani with the thunderbolt; the Buddha restraining the students' jeering; Kanha's marriage to King Okkaka's daughter.

The discourse is a conversation within its own time about birth and status; it should not be framed as a judgment on Hindu tradition today. A Keeper may also wish a Hindu studies reader to check tone.

The Buddha's motive in telling the Kanha story is softened to a reading ('read this way'); the sutta itself has him press Ambattha hard. The script also omits the later section where the Buddha argues that khattiyas rank above brahmins by lineage; a Keeper should confirm that leaving it out is a fair simplification and not a distortion.
Editor review: removed 'his best student' (DN 3 does not rank him); practice no longer tells the listener that everyone has a family pride.
